did_you_know.text: Did you know? Azariah, also called Uzziah, ruled Judah for fifty-two years—one of the longest reigns described in the chapter.

Did you know? Although Azariah did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, he was afflicted with leprosy and lived in a separate house; his son Jotham handled the administration of the people and the affairs of the kingdom.
Did you know? Zechariah ruled Israel for only six months. His murder by Shallum fulfilled the word of the Lord to Jehu that his descendants would sit on the throne to the fourth generation.
Did you know? Shallum, who seized power after murdering Zechariah, also ruled for an extremely short time—one month—until Menahem killed him and succeeded him as king.
Did you know? Menahem brutally suppressed the resistance of Tiphsah after its people refused to open the city gates to him; Scripture describes his actions as part of the kingdom’s decline.
Did you know? Menahem sought to secure his rule by paying a thousand talents of silver to Pul, king of Assyria—evidence that the kings of Israel depended on the support of regional powers.

Did you know? Menahem collected the money for the king of Assyria from the army officers—fifty shekels of silver from each man. After receiving the payment, the king of Assyria withdrew and did not remain in the land.

Did you know? Pekahiah ruled for only two years, until Pekah son of Remaliah, one of his officers, conspired against him and killed him in the royal palace, along with Argob, Arieh, and fifty men from Gilead.

Did you know? In the days of Pekah, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, captured extensive territories in the north, including Galilee and all the land of Naphtali, and deported their inhabitants to Assyria.

Did you know? Jotham did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, and during his reign the upper gate of the house of the Lord was built; however, the high places were not removed, and the people continued to offer sacrifices and burn incense there.
